title: Hunga Tonga: The Eruption That Reached the Edge of Space
description:
On 15 January 2022, the island sitting above the Hunga volcano stopped existing — and the blast that removed it sent a plume straight through the stratosphere and into the mesosphere, higher than anything in the satellite record. Within hours, barometers on every continent were twitching to a pressure pulse that circled the Earth four times, and the water it carried was expected to linger in the stratosphere for years.

thumbnail_concepts.hero: a straight-down satellite view of a vast white eruption plume bursting through an unbroken deck of cloud, the dark blue Pacific visible at the edges of frame
thumbnail_concepts.why_click: It names a height far beyond anything weather reaches, and the arrow forces you to ask what could carry a cloud that high — and how long it took.

thumbnail_concepts.hero: a lone figure silhouetted on a dark Pacific shoreline at dusk, dwarfed by a towering white eruption column on the horizon that is already flattening at the top like an anvil
thumbnail_concepts.why_click: No words, no labels — just a person and a column of ash that has visibly punched through the ceiling of the sky, which makes you click to find out what you're looking at.

thumbnail_concepts.hero: the curved limb of Earth photographed from orbit at night, a faint pale ripple band travelling through the upper atmosphere above the dark ocean
thumbnail_concepts.why_click: A recording indicator on a planet-wide image implies something is still being tracked as it goes round and round — the viewer clicks to find out what kept circulating.
